title: The Secret to Supercharging Learning with Projects
author: Shari Keller
summary: Keller distinguishes ordinary hands-on activities from true project-based learning for the teacher or parent guiding children. Activities usually have kids following instructions toward one right answer, which can crowd out problem-solving, critical thinking and a sense of control. A project instead starts from an open-ended umbrella question that is relevant to the child and cannot simply be Googled. She shows the method with a pumpkin project: mind mapping to generate questions, then a loose pathway of activities in which each child pursues a different angle. The adult becomes a guide who structures the flow rather than supplying answers, and the process, including false steps, counts as much as the product. The piece is an introduction to a series and ends with pointers to her own project materials.
points: Instructions-following activities, even hands-on ones, can miss problem-solving and ownership that projects develop.
A good project starts with an open-ended umbrella question that is relevant to the learner and not answerable by searching.
Mind mapping turns the umbrella question into individual lines of inquiry, so each child's project ends up unique.
The adult acts as guide, structuring the project flow and learning alongside the child rather than holding all the answers.
Because all activities serve the umbrella question, they are relevant in a deeper way, and the process matters as much as the result.
quotes: But let's hit pause for a moment. Traditional activities tend to have kids following a set of instructions.
It's a thought-provoking question about something that is relevant to your child. It has an answer within your child's reach, but it's not something you can Google.

In project based learning, there's no single right answer to a project. Students might ‘follow’ a series of activities, but the activities lead to a goal and every child's project ends up being unique.
I usually start off with mind mapping. I'm a big fan of this process, and I use it for every project. It gets kids thinking about connections, brainstorming, and exploring their own sense of wonder.

You don't need to have all the answers; just a willingness to ask questions, explore, and learn with your child. Your role is to help structure the project flow and guide your child to define the steps and activities to answer the umbrella question.
The activities all have the same purpose—to answer the umbrella question. This makes them relevant in a much deeper way than following instructions.
